content: Blood culture is a microbiological test performed on blood samples to detect infections that are circulating in the bloodstream, such as bacteremia or septicemia. To perform a blood culture, at least 10 milliliters of blood is drawn via venipuncture and distributed into two or more specialized blood bottles containing media designed to support the growth of aerobic and anaerobic microorganisms. It is critical to avoid contamination of the blood samples with bacteria from healthcare staff or other patients. To minimize this risk, the patient’s skin at the venipuncture site is disinfected with denatured alcohol and betadine. Additionally, sterile gloves must be worn during the procedure to further reduce the likelihood of contamination. To improve the diagnostic accuracy of blood cultures, multiple samples are often collected from different venipuncture sites. The probability of identifying the causative organism increases with the volume of blood collected. For example, in cases of suspected infective endocarditis, clinical guidelines may recommend obtaining up to six sets of blood cultures, which equates to approximately 60 milliliters of blood. Blood cultures are commonly ordered by hospital physicians when a patient presents with fever, as this may indicate a systemic infection. Identifying the specific pathogen responsible for the infection allows for the selection of the most appropriate antibiotic therapy and helps address any associated risk factors. Blood cultures are particularly critical in diagnosing infective endocarditis, a condition in which bacteria periodically enter the bloodstream from infected heart valves. In such cases, repeated blood cultures may be necessary, especially during febrile episodes, to capture the transient bacteremia. The development of blood culture techniques dates back to the early 20th century. A notable historical example is the case of composer Gustav Mahler, who was diagnosed with infective endocarditis near the end of his life. Unfortunately, as this occurred before the advent of antibiotics, the disease contributed to his premature death.
